sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Purpose note and imports
sections.what: Explains that this is a regression test for the driver-name guard, and imports the validator and cluster type from the lessons-learnt tool.
sections.why: The header explains that both accepting ordinary words and rejecting invented names must be checked together.
sections.watch_out: Do not tighten the guard without re-running the accept cases.

sections.name: cluster
sections.title: Sample cluster builder
sections.what: Makes a cluster record where every example fact has the same project name and empty URL, with the given text lists as dominant terms.
sections.why: The validator needs a cluster object to check against, and this supplies a minimal one.
sections.watch_out: Example fact ids are generated in order, and the validator checks names against them, so the id order matters.

sections.name: Case
sections.title: Shape of one test case
sections.what: Defines what each case holds: a label, whether it should be accepted or rejected, the sample cluster, the proposed name and rationale, and for rejections the word the reason must contain.
sections.why: The reason check stops a rejection for an unrelated cause from counting as a pass.
sections.watch_out: Only rejections use the reason check, so an accept case that is rejected will show a failure but no reason check.

sections.name: MATERIAL
sections.title: Source text for the guard
sections.what: Three sentences about commissioning and a company acquisition. Any capitalised word in a test name is compared against these sentences.
sections.why: Words present here may be accepted; words absent should be rejected.
sections.watch_out: Editing these sentences can flip several cases, so keep them stable.

sections.name: cases (part 1)
sections.title: Accept cases
sections.what: Four cases that must pass: a sentence-case name made of ordinary words, a rationale starting with This or Several, a Title-Case phrase of common nouns not in the source, and a real company name that the source does mention.
sections.why: The label says these are the false positives the fix targets, meaning ordinary words that were wrongly rejected before.
sections.watch_out: The Title-Case case passes only because those are common English words, so it could fail if the rule becomes stricter about capitals.

sections.name: cases (part 2)
sections.title: Reject cases
sections.what: Six cases that must fail: an invented company, an invented place name, a fabricated company name, a made-up number, a web address, and an invented name placed first in the sentence.
sections.why: The label says the fabrication guard must keep working, and the first-word case stops the sentence-start rule from hiding fakes.
sections.watch_out: The first-word case is the one most likely to break if the sentence-start exception is loosened.

sections.name: cases (part 3)
sections.title: Runs all cases and reports
sections.what: Runs the validator on each case, checks the decision and the reason text for rejections, prints each result, and reports how many passed.
sections.why: One run gives a complete list rather than stopping at the first failure.
sections.watch_out: The reason text is only checked for rejections that define an expected word, so a wrong reason on an accept case is not caught.

summary: Regression test for the guard that rejects invented entity names, such as company or place names, in AI-generated cluster names.
purpose: Makes sure the guard lets through ordinary capitalised English that appears in the source material, and blocks names that do not.
why: The header says the two halves pull in opposite directions, so fixing one can silently break the other. Testing both together catches that.
how: Builds a sample cluster and a short source text. Runs ten cases, each expecting accept or reject, and for rejections checks that the reason names the bad word. Prints a summary count.
inputs: Built-in cases and a built-in source text. No model, gateway or database.
outputs: A PASS or FAIL block per case with the name, decision and reason, then a count such as 10 of 10 passed. Exits 1 if any case fails.
risks: Tightening the guard may reject real names that the material does not mention. Loosening it may let invented names through. The test set is small, so it only covers the cases listed.
debug: Run npx tsx script/verify-proper-noun-guard.ts. Look at the got and reason lines of any failing case. If an accept case is rejected, check whether its words appear in the source text.
